title: Probability & Statistics — Common Core High School Math — Question Sets
id_format: S<set>-<section>-Q<number>. Section codes: M = MAIN (the course's own standard), B1, B2, ... = BACKWARD branches (a Grade K-8 standard, or a course standard that is the MAIN standard of an earlier set), F1 = FORWARD 1 and F2 = FORWARD 2 (standards of later courses; standard_course names the course). id is unique within this collection; uid = "PS:" + id is unique across all collections. Forward branches name standards only, never question IDs of other collections. Set and branch numbers are fixed: they need not be consecutive, and an ID is never reused for a different skill (see revisions.json).

relations.main: the Probability & Statistics skill the set is built around (strand: core, or advanced extension (+))
relations.backward: a prerequisite obstacle to check when a student misses MAIN questions: a Grade K-8, Algebra I or Geometry standard, or the MAIN standard of an earlier set of this course; branch.alignment is exact or supporting
relations.forward1: the next demand after MAIN; branch.progression is same-course deepening, cross-standard extension, or later-course extension, and branch.new_demand states what it adds
relations.forward2: a further demand; branch.builds_on says how it builds on FORWARD 1 (or why it is a separate extension of MAIN)
relations.nearest_related: true marks a forward branch that no standard directly continues; it uses the nearest related standard

grading_rules: Match each student response to its key record by the question ID printed on the question page (for example S12-B2-Q3). The page number is the same in the Question Collection and the Answer Key. IDs are unique within one collection; across collections use uid (for example PS:S12-B2-Q3).

Every question is graded automatically; no question needs a person, a drawing surface, or a judgment of wording. Question types are mc, tf and sa only. There is no partial credit: a response is correct or not.
Multiple choice and true/false: the response is correct when the chosen letter equals correct_letter.

Short answer: the response is checked against correct_answer by the game's answer checker. Mathematically equivalent numbers (fractions, decimals, percents where the question asks for a percent, "x = 5" or "5") are accepted unless the question names a form. When an answer has several parts (one per answer line), every part must be correct. A list of values may be given in any order unless the question says "in that order".
A word answer is used only when the question lists the allowed words (for example "Answer Yes or No"); the response must be one of those words.
grading_note gives the accepted form, the work behind the answer and, for multiple choice, what is wrong with each other choice. It is guidance for teachers, not for students.

Precision: a question that asks for rounding names the precision ("to the nearest hundredth", "as a percent to one decimal place"), and the answer must be given to exactly that precision. A probability may be given as a fraction or a decimal unless the question names one form; a fraction need not be in lowest terms unless the question says so.

Conventions stated on the page: quartiles are the medians of the lower and upper halves (the median left out of both halves when n is odd); an outlier lies more than 1.5·IQR beyond a quartile; each question says whether a standard deviation is the population (divide by n) or sample (divide by n - 1) value; histogram bins include their left endpoint and exclude their right endpoint unless stated otherwise; residual = observed - predicted.

Probability models: every question states the sample space or the process (fair, equally likely, with or without replacement, order matters or not, independent trials), and "or" is inclusive unless stated otherwise.

Simulation: a question that asks students to carry out a simulation supplies the random digits and the rule for using them, so every correct procedure gives the same result. A question about a simulation run by someone else supplies its results. Every inference states the null model, the outcomes counted (one or two tails) and the cutoff; a rare result is evidence against a model, not proof, and a common result is consistent with the model, not proof that it is true.

Skills that ask students to construct a display, design a study or explain a conclusion are assessed by what the game can check: the numbers that define the display (counts, quartiles, residuals), a choice among candidate plots, designs or arguments whose other choices are specific errors, or the conclusion that follows from supplied evidence. COVERAGE.md records which subskills are assessed by recognition.

Technology: a question that needs a calculator or spreadsheet says so and names the capability (mean and standard deviation, least-squares line, correlation, normal area). A normal table is printed on the page when a question uses one.
Every question has an explanation in its grading_note; for numeric questions it shows the work and the exact value.
markup: prompt is plain text. prompt_markup uses {a/b} for a stacked fraction and 2{1/2} for a mixed number.
